essentials: The Batteries Regulation covers the **whole life cycle** of every battery sold in the EU: sourcing, production, use, collection and recycling.
It is the first product law to combine **carbon footprint rules, recycled content targets, a digital passport and supply-chain due diligence**.
Obligations arrive in steps. The **battery passport** becomes mandatory on **18 February 2027**; **raw-material due diligence** on **18 August 2027**, after a two-year postponement.
It is a **regulation**, replacing the 2006 Batteries Directive, so the rules are identical across Member States.

sections.title: Why it exists
text: Demand for batteries is rising fast with electric vehicles and energy storage. Their production is emission-intensive and relies on cobalt, lithium, nickel and graphite, which are linked to environmental damage and labour abuses in some mining regions. The regulation aims to make the batteries that power the transition sustainable themselves and to keep valuable materials in circulation.

sections.title: Five battery categories
points: **Portable batteries**: sealed, up to 5 kg, for example in phones and tools.
**Light means of transport (LMT) batteries**: for e-bikes and e-scooters.
**Starting, lighting and ignition (SLI) batteries**: the classic car battery.
**Industrial batteries**: for industrial uses and energy storage.
**Electric vehicle batteries**: traction batteries for cars and vans.
after: Which obligations apply, and when, depends on the category.

sections.title: Due diligence in detail
text: Companies that place batteries on the market and exceed €40m net turnover must adopt a due diligence policy for the four raw materials, covering social and environmental risks from child labour to water pollution. It follows the OECD guidance: management system, risk identification, risk response, third-party verification and public reporting. A notified body verifies the policy and audits it periodically.
The start was moved from August 2025 to **18 August 2027** because the verification bodies and guidelines were not yet in place.

sections.title: Collection and recycling
points: **Collection of portable batteries**: 63% by the end of 2027 and 73% by the end of 2030.
**Collection of LMT batteries**: 51% by the end of 2028 and 61% by the end of 2031.
**Material recovery**: for lithium, 50% by the end of 2027 and 80% by the end of 2031; high rates for cobalt, copper, lead and nickel.
**No landfilling or incineration** of waste batteries.

sections.title: Who is responsible
text: The regulation addresses **manufacturers**, **importers** and **distributors** as economic operators, and **producers** in the sense of whoever first makes a battery available in a Member State, who carry extended producer responsibility there. Batteries must bear the CE marking and, from 2027, a QR code. National market surveillance authorities enforce the rules.

terms.text: The digital record for an individual battery, accessible through a QR code. The first mandatory digital product passport in EU law.

The share of a material in a new battery that was recovered from waste.
The producer's duty to finance and organise collection and treatment of waste batteries.

practice: **Classify your batteries** by category; this decides which duties and dates apply.
**Determine your role** for each market: manufacturer, importer, distributor, producer.
**Build the data flows for the passport** with cell and material suppliers before 2027.
If above €40m turnover, **prepare the due diligence policy** and engage a notified body.
**Register as a producer** and join a take-back scheme in each Member State where you sell.
For portable devices, **review the design** for user-replaceable batteries.

quiz.q: What is new about the scope of the Batteries Regulation compared with the old directive?
options: It covers the whole life cycle, from raw materials to recycling
It applies only to batteries made in the EU
quiz.why: The 2006 directive focused on end of life. The regulation adds sourcing, carbon footprint, design and information.

quiz.q: For which batteries does the battery passport become mandatory on 18 February 2027?
options: Electric vehicle, LMT and industrial batteries above 2 kWh
Only batteries imported from outside the EU
quiz.why: The passport applies to these three groups. Portable and SLI batteries are not covered.

quiz.q: Which raw materials are subject to due diligence?
options: Cobalt, natural graphite, lithium and nickel
quiz.why: These four are the battery raw materials listed. The 3TG minerals fall under the Conflict Minerals Regulation.

quiz.q: From when do the due diligence obligations apply?
quiz.why: The original date of August 2025 was postponed by two years.

quiz.q: What does the removability rule require from February 2027?
options: Batteries in electric vehicles must be swappable
Portable batteries must be removable and replaceable by the end user
All batteries must be removable by robots
Batteries must be removed before export
quiz.why: End users must be able to remove and replace portable batteries in products, which affects product design.

quiz.q: Above which turnover does the due diligence duty apply?
quiz.why: €40m net turnover, far below the CSDDD threshold of €1.5bn.

quiz.q: Why do the rules not differ between Member States?
options: Because it is a regulation, directly applicable
Because batteries are only made in one country
Because the Commission enforces it alone
quiz.why: The 2006 directive needed transposition. The regulation applies directly, though national authorities enforce it.
